Interpretation
The client's score indicates severe dissociative experiences consistent with levels typically seen
in dissociative disorders. They are likely experiencing substantial disruptions in consciousness,
memory, identity, and perception that cause significant impairment in daily functioning. Their
score is higher than 99.9% of the general population. This level of dissociation strongly suggests
further comprehensive assessment for a possible dissociative disorder.

Area(s) of Difficulty:
The responses on the Depersonalisation/Derealisation subscale reflect severe experiences of
feeling disconnected from oneself or perceiving the world as unreal or distorted. These
experiences may include feeling as though they are watching themselves from a distance,
feeling that their body does not belong to them, or perceiving familiar environments as strange
and unfamiliar. In therapy, grounding techniques and mindfulness practices that focus on
present-moment awareness may be beneficial for reducing these symptoms.
Items with the highest ratings were:
- 7. Some people sometimes have the experience of feeling as though they are standing next to
themselves or watching themselves do something and they actually see themselves as if they
were looking at another person. (70%)
- 28. Some people sometimes feel as if they are looking at the world through a fog, so that
people and objects appear far away or unclear. (70%)
- 11. Some people have the experience of looking in a mirror and not recognizing themselves.
The responses on the Amnesia subscale indicate severe difficulties with memory gaps and
forgetting important personal information or events. This pattern of amnesia may involve finding
unfamiliar items among personal belongings, being told about doing things they don't remember,
or having gaps in awareness while performing activities like driving. In therapy, exploration of
these memory disruptions may be important, particularly in the context of any reported trauma
history.
Items with the highest ratings were:
- 8. Some people are told that they sometimes do not recognize friends or family members.
- 5. Some people have the experience of finding new things among their belongings that they do
not remember buying. (50%)
- 26. Some people sometimes find writings, drawings, or notes among their belongings that they
must have done but cannot remember doing. (50%)
The responses on the Absorption subscale indicate substantial tendency to become highly
engrossed in activities or fantasy to the point of reduced awareness of surroundings. While
some absorption can be adaptive (such as in creative pursuits), high levels may indicate using
absorption as a coping mechanism to avoid distress. In therapy, developing awareness of when
this occurs and expanding their repertoire of coping strategies may be helpful.

Scoring and Interpretation Information
The DES-II is scored by calculating the mean of all 28 items, resulting in an overall score and
subscale scores ranging from 0 to 100. Higher scores indicate greater frequency and severity of
dissociative experiences.
Three subscale scores can also be calculated:
Amnesia (items 3, 4, 5, 8, 25, 26): assesses gaps in memory and awareness, with examples
including not knowing how you got somewhere, being dressed in clothes you don’t remember
putting on, finding new things among belongings you don’t remember buying, not recognising
friends or family members, finding evidence of having done things you don’t remember doing.
Depersonalisation/derealisation (items 7, 11, 12, 13, 27, 28): measures feelings of unreality or
detachment regarding oneself or the environment. Examples include feeling that you are
standing next to yourself or watching yourself do something and seeing yourself as if you were
looking at another person, or feeling your body does not belong to you.
Absorption (items 2, 14, 15, 17, 18, 20): measures high engagement in an activity with reduced
awareness of surroundings, related primarily to one’s traumatic experiences. Examples include
realising that you did not hear part or all of what was said by another, remembering a past event
so vividly that you feel as if you are reliving the event, or becoming so involved in a fantasy or
daydream that it feels as though it were really happening to you.
Descriptors based upon the score are also provided:
Low (0-11): Typical in the general population, reflective of normal variations in attention and
awareness.
Mild (12-19): Above community averages but generally remaining within normal limits.
Moderate (20-29): Notable dissociative experiences.
High (30-45): Substantial dissociative symptoms consistent with possible dissociative disorders
Very High (46+): Extreme dissociative experiences, most commonly observed in dissociative
identity disorders.
The total score is also expressed as a percentile rank, based on normative data from van
Ijzendoorn & Schuengel's (1996) meta-analysis of community samples. This percentile
contextualises the client's score relative to the general population, indicating the percentage of
individuals who scored lower than the client. For example, a score at the 85th percentile means

Scoring and Interpretation Information (cont.)
that 85% of people in the community sample scored lower than the client, placing them in the
upper range of dissociative experiences.
When the DES-II score exceeds 30, further assessment for a dissociative disorder is
recommended, potentially including structured clinical interviews such as the Structured Clinical
Interview for DSM-5 Dissociative Disorders (SCID-D) (Steinberg, 1994). It should be noted that a
threshold of 30 has been observed to miss 46% of positive diagnoses of dissociative disorders
later identified via diagnostic interview, so considering a reduced cut off of 20 (Moderate range
or above) will yield higher sensitivity (Leed et al., 2022).
For tracking clinical progress, a reliable change index quantifies a clinically meaningful change
(11 average score points), following guidelines Jacobson and Truax (1991). Monitoring scores
over time allows clinicians to assess treatment effectiveness and adjust interventions as needed.
On first administration a bar graph showing total and subscale average scores is displayed,
along with two comparison graphs illustrating the client's scores relative to different reference
groups. When the assessment is administered multiple times, longitudinal line graphs are
generated to track changes in both total average scores and subscale average scores over time.
